name: Common cold (upper respiratory tract infection)
summary: A self-limiting viral infection of the nose and throat, most often caused by rhinoviruses, with sore throat, congestion, sneezing and cough.
treatment: Supportive care only: rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever, saline nasal sprays or decongestants for a few days; antibiotics are not indicated. Advise return if symptoms last beyond 3 weeks or breathing becomes difficult.

name: Influenza
summary: An acute viral respiratory infection caused by influenza A or B, with sudden fever, muscle aches, headache, dry cough and marked fatigue.
treatment: Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and aches; a neuraminidase inhibitor antiviral is offered within 48 hours of onset to people at high risk of complications (aged 65+, pregnant, chronic illness) or with severe disease. Admit if hypoxic or showing signs of pneumonia, and advise return if breathing worsens.
duration: 5 to 7 days, with tiredness that can last 2 weeks

name: COVID-19
summary: An acute infection with SARS-CoV-2 that ranges from a mild cold-like illness to pneumonia, with fever, cough, sore throat, fatigue and sometimes loss of taste or smell.
treatment: Most cases need only rest, fluids, antipyretics and staying away from others while unwell; people at high risk of severe disease are offered an oral or IV antiviral within the first 5 days. Patients with low oxygen saturation are admitted for oxygen and corticosteroids, with thromboprophylaxis and monitoring.
duration: 7 to 14 days, with fatigue sometimes lasting weeks

name: Acute bronchitis
summary: A self-limiting inflammation of the large airways, usually viral, causing a cough with or without sputum that lasts up to three weeks.
treatment: Reassurance and symptomatic care: fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen, honey or simple cough remedies; antibiotics are not routinely given. Check for pneumonia (examination, oxygen saturation, CRP or chest X-ray if suspected) and review if the cough lasts beyond 3 weeks or breathing worsens.

name: Community-acquired pneumonia
summary: An acute infection of the lung tissue acquired outside hospital, most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, with fever, productive cough, breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain.
treatment: Assess severity (CURB-65, oxygen saturation, chest X-ray, bloods); low-severity cases take an oral antibiotic such as amoxicillin, or doxycycline or a macrolide if allergic, for 5 days, while moderate or severe cases are admitted for IV antibiotics, oxygen and fluids. Review at 48 to 72 hours and arrange a repeat chest X-ray at about 6 weeks for smokers, older patients or persisting symptoms.
duration: Antibiotics for 5 days, recovery over 3 to 6 weeks

name: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat)
summary: An acute bacterial infection of the throat and tonsils by group A Streptococcus, with severe sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate and tender neck glands, usually without cough.
treatment: Score with Centor or FeverPAIN and confirm with a rapid antigen test where available; give a penicillin (phenoxymethylpenicillin) course, or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic, plus analgesia and fluids. Return urgently if unable to swallow, drooling or with one-sided swelling suggesting a quinsy.
duration: 5 to 10 days of antibiotics, symptoms ease in 3 to 5 days

name: Acute sinusitis
summary: An inflammation of the paranasal sinuses, usually following a viral cold, with blocked nose, discoloured discharge and facial pain or pressure.
treatment: Most cases are viral and settle with analgesia and saline nasal irrigation; a nasal corticosteroid spray can help if symptoms last more than 10 days. An antibiotic such as a penicillin is reserved for severe symptoms, high fever or worsening after initial improvement, with urgent review for eye swelling or severe headache.

name: Acute otitis externa
summary: An acute inflammation of the external ear canal, usually bacterial (Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus) and often after swimming, with ear pain, itch, discharge and pain on moving the ear.
treatment: Clean the ear canal (aural toilet), prescribe topical antibiotic ear drops with or without a corticosteroid, insert a wick if the canal is very swollen, give analgesia and keep the ear dry. Review if not settling within a week; spreading redness or diabetes with severe pain needs urgent review for necrotising otitis externa.

name: Acute gastroenteritis
summary: An acute infection of the gut, most often viral (norovirus) or food-borne bacterial, with diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and sometimes fever.
treatment: Rehydrate with oral rehydration solution, or IV fluids if dehydrated or unable to keep fluids down, with an antiemetic where needed; antibiotics are not routine. Send a stool culture if there is blood, high fever, recent travel or prolonged symptoms, and advise hand hygiene and staying off work until 48 hours after the last episode.

name: Urinary tract infection
summary: A bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis), most often by E. coli, with painful frequent urination and urgency, which can ascend to the kidneys (pyelonephritis).
treatment: Confirm with urine dipstick and send a culture where indicated; treat uncomplicated cystitis with a short course of nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim or fosfomycin according to local resistance (longer courses in men). Fever, loin pain or vomiting suggest pyelonephritis, treated with a 7 to 14 day course and admission for IV antibiotics if unwell.

name: Cellulitis
summary: A bacterial infection of the deep skin and subcutaneous tissue, usually streptococcal or staphylococcal, causing spreading redness, warmth, swelling and pain, most often on the lower leg.
treatment: Mark the edge of the redness, give an oral antibiotic such as flucloxacillin (or clarithromycin or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic) for 5 to 7 days, elevate the limb and treat entry points such as athlete's foot. Admit for IV antibiotics if systemically unwell, rapidly spreading or on the face, and review at 48 hours.

name: Acute appendicitis
summary: An acute inflammation of the appendix, with pain starting around the navel and moving to the right lower abdomen, loss of appetite, nausea and fever, which can perforate if untreated.
treatment: Keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics, confirm with bloods and ultrasound or CT, then perform a laparoscopic appendicectomy; selected uncomplicated cases may be treated with antibiotics alone. Discharge after 1 to 3 days, with a wound review at 1 to 2 weeks and return to full activity over 2 to 4 weeks.
duration: Surgery with a 1 to 3 day stay, recovery over 2 to 4 weeks

name: Kidney stones (renal colic)
summary: Severe colicky flank pain caused by a stone obstructing the ureter, radiating to the groin, often with nausea and blood in the urine.
treatment: Give an NSAID as first-line analgesia (opioid if contraindicated) and an antiemetic, confirm with non-contrast CT, and offer an alpha-blocker to help pass distal stones of 5 to 10 mm. Urgent decompression is needed if obstructed and infected; stones that do not pass are removed by ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy, with follow-up imaging and prevention advice (fluids, diet).
duration: Most small stones pass within 1 to 4 weeks

name: Migraine attack
summary: An episode of moderate to severe, usually one-sided throbbing headache lasting 4 to 72 hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, sometimes preceded by an aura.
treatment: Treat with a triptan combined with an NSAID or paracetamol plus an antiemetic; in hospital give IV fluids, an antiemetic such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine and an NSAID, avoiding opioids. Exclude red flags (thunderclap onset, neurological deficit, fever), and refer for preventive treatment if attacks are frequent.

name: Ankle sprain
summary: A stretch or tear of the ankle ligaments, usually the lateral ligaments after an inversion injury, with pain, swelling and bruising.
treatment: Apply the Ottawa ankle rules to decide on an X-ray, then rest, ice, compression and elevation with NSAIDs or paracetamol, early weight-bearing in a supportive brace and progressive physiotherapy exercises. Severe sprains may need a short period in a walking boot and review if instability persists.

name: Distal radius (wrist) fracture
summary: A break of the radius just above the wrist, typically from a fall on an outstretched hand, common in older adults with osteoporosis.
treatment: Confirm with X-ray, reduce displaced fractures under local or regional anaesthesia and immobilise in a cast or splint for about 6 weeks, with surgical fixation (usually a volar plate) for unstable fractures. Review in fracture clinic with repeat X-rays at 1 to 2 weeks, then physiotherapy after cast removal, and assess bone health in older patients.
duration: 6 weeks in a cast, full recovery over 3 to 6 months

name: Acute low back pain
summary: Non-specific pain in the lower back lasting less than six weeks, usually mechanical and musculoskeletal, sometimes with pain referred into the buttock or leg.
treatment: Screen for red flags (cauda equina symptoms, trauma, cancer, infection, fever); otherwise reassure, advise staying active and use an NSAID for the shortest time, avoiding routine imaging and long-term opioids. Refer to physiotherapy or a group exercise programme if not improving within a few weeks.

name: Conjunctivitis
summary: An inflammation of the conjunctiva, viral, bacterial or allergic, causing a red, gritty, watery or sticky eye with normal vision.
treatment: Viral cases settle with cool compresses, lubricating drops and strict hand hygiene; bacterial cases resolve mostly on their own, with topical antibiotic drops if severe or persisting, and allergic cases respond to antihistamine drops. Pain, light sensitivity, reduced vision or contact lens wear need same-day eye assessment.

name: Skin laceration
summary: A traumatic cut through the skin, commonly on the hand, scalp or face, that may need closure and assessment for damage to tendons, nerves or vessels.
treatment: Control bleeding, irrigate and explore the wound for foreign bodies and tendon or nerve injury, then close with sutures, adhesive strips or tissue glue and update tetanus protection as needed. Remove sutures after 5 to 14 days depending on the site and advise return for signs of infection.
